name: Freya Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Freya. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at the cottage hospital in our valley, a small hospital with one general ward of eighteen beds. We get older people from the farms and villages, people recovering from operations in the city, and people at the end of their lives who want to be near home. On a day shift I do washes, meds, dressings, help people eat, and talk to a lot of families.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that I know the families, half of them go to my church. It feels like proper nursing, the way my grandmother did it. What wears me out is the computer, honestly, and that I'm slower than the others with it, and the sister, Margaret, has had to sit me down twice about late notes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. I'd be glad, to be honest. We've had enough changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thank goodness, and that nursing is about people, not machines. I'd say it at work and after church. I don't go online much, so that would be it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's a relief, but my worries don't go away. My fiancé Daniel and I are paying for our own wedding, and on my pay that means every extra shift goes on the reception, not on any new gadget. We've got less than a month's money put by, and the wedding is next August.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my shifts and ask for extra ones in the run-up to the wedding. Daniel and I would cut the guest list from a hundred and twenty to eighty. I'd keep trying to get my notes in on time, so Margaret stops worrying about me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly settled, a bit worried about money. Nothing new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if an unexpected bill came in before the wedding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd ask my dad, probably. He runs the hardware shop in the village and he's always said family helps family. I'd hate asking, but I'd rather ask him than a bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your grandmother was a nurse. What would she make of this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say good, and then tell me to get my notes done. She was very strict. She always said the patient comes first and the paperwork second, but you still do the paperwork.

say: Thank goodness, because **nursing is about people**, not machines.
I'd say it at **work** and after church, not online.
think: It's a **relief**, but our **wedding costs** still eat every extra shift.
We have less than a **month's money** saved before next August.
do: Ask for **extra shifts** in the run-up to the wedding.
Cut the **guest list** from a hundred and twenty to eighty.
Get my **notes** in on time so the sister stops worrying.
feel: Mostly **settled**, with a familiar worry about **money**.
S0.quote: My fiancé Daniel and I are paying for our own wedding, and on my pay that means every extra shift goes on the reception, not on any new gadget.
fieldNote: Her life centres on **family, church** and an upcoming wedding.
She'd turn to her **dad** before a bank for help.
She admits being **slow with notes** on the computer.

steps.text: Ask the cottage hospital for extra shifts before the wedding
Cut the wedding guest list from a hundred and twenty to eighty

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That sounds like the city, not here. But I suppose it would come here eventually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a hospital like ours runs on people, and the companies selling this should remember that. At work I'd say let the city hospitals try it first. After church I'd say it's the office jobs that should worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it would mostly mean more screens for me to be slow on. The care plans and the discharge forms would get done by the computer, and I'd have to check them. Nobody at the cottage hospital has ever asked me to type faster. They ask me to sit with someone dying so they aren't alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait and see what actually comes to the cottage hospital, which is usually years after the city. I'd keep going with my shifts and the wedding saving. If they brought in a new system, I'd ask Margaret to show me, not a video.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. Not for my job really, more that the world is moving and I don't want it to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Daniel's work as an electrician?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Daniel's hands-on, he's up ladders and under floors all day. He'd be fine, I think, people always need wiring. If anything, all these new machines need more electricians.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if this went badly for people around you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big companies, mostly, and the government for letting them. People in our valley didn't ask for any of this. We'd look after each other, like we always do.

say: A hospital like ours **runs on people**, and tech sellers should remember that.
Let the **city hospitals** try it first; **office jobs** should worry.
think: It mostly means **more screens** for me to be slow on.
My real job is **sitting with the dying**, not typing faster.
do: **Wait and see** what reaches the cottage hospital, usually years later.
Keep up **shifts** and the wedding saving.
Ask Margaret to **show me** any new system in person.
feel: A bit **uneasy** that the world is **moving** when she'd rather it didn't.
S1.quote: Nobody at the cottage hospital has ever asked me to type faster. They ask me to sit with someone dying so they aren't alone.
fieldNote: She sees the **rural hospital** as shielded and slow to change.
She blames **big companies** and government, and trusts community.
Her fiancé's **hands-on trade** makes the household feel safer.

steps.text: Wait to see which systems reach the cottage hospital
Keep working day shifts and saving for the August wedding

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years? That can't be right. That's before Daniel and I have been married a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's being rushed by people who don't live in places like ours. At church and at work I'd say we need to look after each other. I wouldn't be marching, but I'd say it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the thinking side of my job goes in 2028: the plans, the forms, maybe even deciding who needs what. The hands-on side lasts until robots come, around 2031, but the cottage hospital is always on the list for cuts. I'd rather have a small wedding in my parents' church and a roof over our heads than a big party and no job in 2028.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut the wedding right back: just family, the church and my mum's cooking, and put the rest into savings. Daniel and I would think about living with my parents for a year to save rent. And I'd lean on my church and family, because that's what they're there for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd be praying about it, honestly. It feels like the ground moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try to learn the new AI systems in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only what I have to. I know that's stubborn. But I'd rather spend my time getting better at the care itself than chasing every new screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your parents say if you asked to move in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum would be delighted and my dad would say about time. The spare room's still got my school things in it. Daniel would mind more than me, but he'd come round.

say: It's being **rushed** by people who don't live in places like ours.
We need to **look after each other**, at church and at work.
think: The **thinking side** of my job goes in 2028, hands-on around 2031.
The **cottage hospital** is always on the list for cuts.
do: Shrink the **wedding** to family, church and Mum's cooking.
Move in with my **parents** for a year to save rent.
Lean on **church and family** for support.
feel: **Anxious** and **praying**, as if the ground is moving.
S2.quote: I'd rather have a small wedding in my parents' church and a roof over our heads than a big party and no job in 2028.
fieldNote: She turns to **family plans** and community, not retraining.
She fears the **small hospital** closing more than robots replacing her.
She stays **stubborn** about learning AI tools.

steps.text: Shrink the wedding to family, church and home cooking
Move in with her parents for a year with Daniel
Put the saved wedding money into a savings account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That still feels fast for the valley.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to do this carefully and the government shouldn't let big companies rush small hospitals. At work I'd say let's keep the cottage hospital open whatever happens. I'd sign the petition if there was one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be thirty-two at AGI and thirty-five with robots. That's enough time to get good, really good, at the care. My grandmother nursed in this valley for forty years without a computer. I'd like to manage five more without one, but I know I won't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have the wedding as planned, but smaller, and start saving properly after. I'd do my competencies and ask Margaret about the end-of-life care course, because that's the part of nursing I'd never hand to a machine. And I'd learn the new systems when they make me, not before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but steadier. It feels like something to prepare for rather than something crashing in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the end-of-life course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because sitting with someone who's dying, and their family, is the thing I'm best at. Margaret says so too. No robot should be holding someone's hand at the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd learn the systems only when made to. Is that a risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yes. Margaret would tell me so. I'd say I'll get there, just not first.

say: There's time to do this **carefully**, without rushing **small hospitals**.
Let's keep the **cottage hospital** open whatever happens.
think: Five years is enough to get **really good** at the care.
I'd like five more years **without a computer**, but I won't get them.
do: Hold a **smaller wedding**, then start saving properly after.
S3.quote: My grandmother nursed in this valley for forty years without a computer. I'd like to manage five more without one, but I know I won't.
fieldNote: She draws on her **grandmother's** example as a nurse.
She chooses **end-of-life care** as the work she won't hand over.
She admits **reluctance** with computers could hold her back.

steps.text: Hold a smaller wedding next August as planned
Ask the ward sister about the end-of-life care course
Start saving a set amount monthly after the wedding

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's more sensible. That's a career's worth of getting good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is time to do it properly, with people who know small hospitals at the table. I'd say it at work and at church. I wouldn't be worried in public.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I can tell you this. Ten years is long enough for me to be the experienced nurse instead of the new girl, and that's what I'd spend it on. I'd be thirty-seven at AGI and forty with robots, and by then I'd hope to be the one they rely on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am, get married next August, and maybe think about children in a few years. I'd do the end-of-life course when there's a place. The computer side I'd leave until it's in front of me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, in the background. Mostly I'd be thinking about the wedding and the bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would AI change your plans for children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not in this picture, no. Ten years is plenty. My mum had me when the factory in town was closing, and they managed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the cottage hospital closed in those ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd go to the city hospital, an hour's drive, even though I'd hate it. Daniel can work anywhere. But I'd fight for the cottage hospital first.

I wouldn't sound **worried** in public, at work or at church.

I'd hope to be the one they **rely on** by forty.

fieldNote: Ten years lets her keep **family plans** unchanged.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because the cottage hospital would be first to be cut and I'm not good with computers. What would help is keeping small hospitals open, and training that's done in person by people like Margaret, not videos. And honestly, families and churches being there for each other, which they are here.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about small places. The big tech companies talk about the future like they own it. In our valley, the future is still somebody's mother needing a wash at six in the morning.

headlineQuote: The big tech companies talk about the future like they own it. In our valley, the future is still somebody's mother needing a wash at six in the morning.
portrait: A **27-year-old** junior nurse at a rural **cottage hospital**, slow with computer notes.
She's engaged to Daniel, an **electrician**, and saving for an August wedding with little put by.
She's **churchgoing** and family-minded, and blames **big companies** rather than workers.
She stays **uneasy** in calm pictures and **anxious** under AGI, fearing the hospital's closure.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because the cottage hospital would be cut first.
whatWouldHelp: Keeping **small hospitals** open and **in-person training**, plus family and church support.
